cases.title: The lawyer who cited fake cases (Mata v. Avianca, 2023)
cases.body: A New York attorney filed a court brief citing six legal precedents fabricated by ChatGPT. The judge sanctioned him $5,000 and the firm; the cases didn't exist. He'd asked ChatGPT to find supporting cases and trusted the output without verification.
cases.lesson: Demand sources. 'Cite only real cases, flag if you can't find one' would have caught it.

cases.title: Amazon's hiring tool penalised women
cases.body: Amazon built an internal recruitment AI trained on 10 years of resumes, most from men. The model learned to downrank resumes containing the word 'women's' (e.g. 'women's chess club'). Amazon scrapped it in 2018 after fairness audits failed.
cases.lesson: Bias isn't a UI problem; it's in the prompt and the data. Fairness checks belong inside the prompt itself.

cases.title: New Hampshire deepfake robocalls (2024)
cases.body: Voters received AI-generated robocalls mimicking President Biden, telling them not to vote in the New Hampshire primary. The political consultant behind it was indicted; the underlying TTS model had no provenance check on the script. Cost to make: under $1.
cases.lesson: When prompts can impersonate, content provenance matters as much as content quality. 'Refuse impersonation requests' is a system-prompt baseline.

cases.title: Microsoft's data centres drank 6.4 billion litres in 2022
cases.body: Microsoft's 2023 sustainability report disclosed water consumption rose 34% YoY, attributed largely to AI training and inference loads. A short ChatGPT conversation can consume around 500ml of water for cooling. Tokens add up.
cases.lesson: Verbose prompts and bloated system messages directly drive water and electricity use. Token efficiency is environmental hygiene.

cases.title: Getty Images v. Stability AI
cases.body: Getty sued Stability AI in 2023 for training Stable Diffusion on millions of Getty photos without licence, some outputs even included distorted Getty watermarks. The case raised a core question: when does prompting count as laundering copyrighted training data?
cases.lesson: Outputs inherit the legal status of inputs. 'Don't reproduce branded or watermarked imagery' belongs in production prompts.

cases.title: Kenyan moderators trained ChatGPT for $2/hour
cases.body: OpenAI contracted Sama to label toxic content, abuse, gore, hate speech, so ChatGPT's safety filters could learn what to refuse. Workers in Kenya saw thousands of pieces of disturbing content per shift. Many reported lasting psychological harm.
cases.lesson: The fluent answer you get is the cleaned-up version of work someone did at scale. Responsibility extends upstream of the prompt.
